1:
The date of the vision raises a question about where the chapter belongs. Adam Clarke reports that most interpreters take it for the first of Isaiah’s prophecies, since it seems to contain his solemn designation to the office, but doubts it: the prophet is said to have prophesied in the reign of Uzziah and to have written that king’s acts, which a contemporary would do; the phrase in the year that Uzziah died probably means after his death, as it does of another king elsewhere; and the prophecies are not in order of time, since four later chapters seem by internal marks to be older than the first. John Calvin reports a stronger version of the same view, that this is really the beginning of the book and that an error was made in collecting the prophecies, the ground being that the prophet here declines the office, seems a novice unacquainted with his calling, and says that he has now seen the Lord. Calvin calls these reasons feeble. It is not strange, he answers, that a man so overpowered by an extraordinary vision should forget he was a prophet, since no feeling in him escaped the presence of God, so that like one who had lost his senses he plunged himself into darkness, or rather like one despairing of life chose to die; and the godly ought to be so affected when God gives them tokens of his presence.

Charles Ellicott puts the vision just before the king’s death, on the ground that the first year of his successor would have been the more natural formula afterwards, and allows that the narrative may have been written later and set here deliberately, so that readers might see what the prophet saw, and find in the preceding chapters the development of what he had then heard. He fills in the moment: twenty years of outward prosperity with much inward corruption; a king who had profaned the temple now either just dead or dragging out the dregs of his leprous life in seclusion; an earthquake that had left a vague sense of impending judgment; and the question of what was to become of the people pressing on the prophet. He thinks it significant that Isaiah’s first work as a writer was the history of that reign. John Gill gives the year in three reckonings, the fifty-second of the reign, the year 3246 from the creation, and, on the authority of a father, the year in which the founder of Rome was born; and he reports that some take the death not literally but of the leprosy that struck the king when he tried to burn incense, after which he was shut up apart, a kind of civil death.

Matthew Henry asks what the vision was for and gives two answers: to confirm the prophet’s faith, so that he might himself be satisfied of the truth of what was afterwards revealed, and to work upon his affections, so that reverence might both quicken him and fix him to his service, since those who teach others the knowledge of God ought to be well acquainted with him themselves. He notes that the vision is dated for the greater certainty of it, and makes the date itself preach: when the breath of princes goes forth and they return to their earth, our comfort is that the Lord reigns for ever, so that the king dies while the God of that people still lives, and the mortality of great and good men should send us to look up to the King eternal. John Wesley adds only that the Lord seen is the Divine Majesty as he subsists in three persons, and that the train is a royal and judicial robe, since he is represented here as a judge.
2:
The seraphim are identified differently by each voice. Charles Ellicott notes that this is their only appearance among the heavenly host, the word elsewhere naming the fiery serpents of the wilderness; here there is no trace of serpent form, nor of the animal forms of the cherubim, the burning ones being men in likeness, with six wings. He records the old distinction between seraphim that excel in love and cherubim that excel in knowledge, and notes that it rests on the etymology. John Gill rejects three readings, that they are the Son and the Spirit, that they are the two Testaments, and that they are angels, which he calls the common interpretation; he makes them ministers of the Gospel, and reports that Jewish commentators identify them with the living creatures of the other vision. John Calvin inclines to two, answering to the cherubim over the ark, but will not assert where Scripture is silent, remembering that another prophet saw thousands of thousands.

Keil and Delitzsch settle what kind of seeing this was. The prophet was not asleep; God opened in him, while awake, an inner sense for what is above sense while the outer senses slept; and though other visions show the earthly temple, here the throne is its heavenly original, so that the prophet is carried up. Adam Clarke takes up the covered feet, explaining that the Hebrews mean by them the whole lower part of the body, and that where robes reached the ground bare feet were thought indecent; he supports this from a traveller who saw an eastern king sitting cross-legged, his robe drawn over his unshod feet for decency. John Wesley keeps the name to its meaning of fire, standing for the nature of these beings or their fervent zeal.

On the threefold cry the question is how it was sung. Keil and Delitzsch deny that all sang together and describe a continuous antiphon, one company beginning and the others answering. Clarke gives the practice a history, alternate singing running from the ode at the sea to the time of Ezra. Ellicott allows that the repetition may mark the mode of utterance, antiphonal and then in chorus, or may be the Hebrew idiom of emphasis by threefold iteration; from a later standpoint, he adds, readers have found in it the glory of God in past and present and future, or a faint foreshadowing of the Trinity, but historically it cannot be separated from the name of the Holy One of Israel. Calvin draws the lesson that the angels are set before us for imitation, the holiest service we can render being praise, and that God associates us with them so that we may resemble the inhabitants of heaven.

The shaking and the smoke close the scene. Keil and Delitzsch place the prophet as far from the throne as possible, under the door of the heavenly temple, and render the shaken parts not as lintels, with the old versions, but as the foundations of the thresholds, supporting the word from a rabbinic use of it for a hand-mill frame. Ellicott agrees, placing him before the holiest place. On the smoke he offers two readings, that it answers the smoke as of a furnace on the mount and stands for wrath as the brightness of the throne stands for love, or that it is the incense-smoke that elsewhere symbolises prayer, though then censers would have been mentioned. Calvin makes the noise a proof that the voice was not human, since no mortal voice can shake a building, and adds that if dumb creatures are moved, much more should we be. Gill reports that some connect it with the earthquake of that reign, but answers with a rabbi that the moving was in the vision and not in fact; Wesley calls such motions tokens of anger, and the smoke, elsewhere a sign of acceptance, a sign of anger.
5:
The cry turns on a single word. Adam Clarke will not have undone, and renders it I am become dumb, from a root meaning to be silent, reporting that twenty-eight manuscripts, three editions and three old versions support it. John Calvin takes the same view and wonders why one father rendered it otherwise, since the passive form is plainly marked; the prophet was so terrified as to resemble a dead man. Men imagine that they live, he says, swelled with vain confidence, because they do not know God; until he reveals himself we think ourselves not men but gods, and only when we have seen him do we begin to know what we are, which is where true humility springs from. Keil and Delitzsch supply the reason: the holiness of God is to a sinner a consuming fire, and the distance between creature and Creator is of itself prostrating, as the seraphim showed by veiling their faces.

Charles Ellicott sets the cry among its parallels, the lawgiver hiding his face and the fisherman asking his Lord to depart; but he finds a contrast as well. The lawgiver at his call felt chiefly the want of utterance, whereas here the thought is of lips defiled by past sins of speech: how shall a man join the praises of the seraphim with lips from which bitter words and formal prayers have come? Those lips are unclean as the lips of one stricken with leprosy, as the dead king had been. Matthew Henry is struck by the reversal: one would have expected the man so favoured to call himself blessed, and instead he cries that he is a gone man, silenced, struck dumb. John Wesley makes him an unclean branch of an unclean tree, involved by omission and commission in the guilt of his people, and John Gill allows that a good man may think himself miserable, partly for his own corruptions and partly for the company he keeps.

The live coal is treated as a sacrament. Keil and Delitzsch call the forgiveness a heavenly sacrament conveyed by a seraphic absolution, note that the flight of one implies a large and indefinite number, and leave open whether what was taken with the tongs was a red-hot stone or a burning coal. Ellicott presses further. The altar is commonly taken for the heavenly one, but he finds a deeper meaning if the seraph came to the altar of incense beside which the prophet stood, so that what had seemed formal worship was quickened with living power and the symbol became sacramental. Fire, he observes, is throughout the Bible the sign at once of wrath and love, destroying the evil and purifying the good, so that the prophet passed through the purgatory of an instantaneous agony. Clarke keeps to the altar of burnt-offering, on which the fire that first came down from heaven burned perpetually, and makes the coal the word of prophecy put into the prophet’s mouth.

Calvin guards the transaction. The coal had no virtue of its own, as superstitious men imagine of the magical arts; the angel administered the cleansing but was not its author. The sign was useful all the same, since we are not angels who behold the mysteries of God unassisted, and this is the use of sacraments, to strengthen us in proportion to our ignorance. He answers an objection, that it is absurd to cleanse a tongue the Spirit had already used: the Lord had cleansed him before, but by degree, and this cleansing is greater because God meant to raise him to higher dignity among the people. Ellicott divides the absolution into pardon and purity, the conditions of his work and of his own completeness. Wesley notes that the coal touched the lips without burning them, and Gill that forgiving sin is God’s act alone while preaching forgiveness is his ministers’ work.
8:
The voice asking whom it shall send is heard by a changed man. Charles Ellicott says the cleansing has made the prophet one of the heavenly brotherhood, an angel called to an angel’s work: he had seen the glory and been overwhelmed, and now hears the voice and is roused. The mixture of singular and plural in the question occupies him next. It cannot be a plural of majesty, he argues, since the great kings of the east always spoke of themselves in the singular, that usage being the invention of a later and more servile court; part of the explanation is that God is here a king in council; but Christian thought, he adds, has scarcely erred in finding a foreshadowing of a plurality within the Unity. Keil and Delitzsch reach the council and stop there, refusing three explanations, self-consultation, a plural of majesty, and an abstract plural, and referring it to the seraphim, who with the Lord form one deliberative body. John Wesley calls the change of number very remarkable and takes it to intimate a plurality of persons in the Godhead.

John Calvin asks why God should speak as though he could not find a qualified man. Some take it for a reproof of the ignorance of the priests, which he allows to be probable; but he prefers the certainty of the calling, since the deliberation shows the appointment was made by choice and not at random. God does not hesitate; such ways of speaking are used on our account. John Gill notes that one paraphrase makes the speaker the Word of the Lord rather than the Father.

Then comes the commission, and every voice feels its weight. Keil and Delitzsch put the paradox sharply: the seraph absolved the prophet with the burning coal so that he might not absolve but harden his people by his word, the terrible opposite of the mission he had just experienced in himself; and they note that this people points back to the people of unclean lips among whom he had complained of dwelling. Ellicott says no harder task was perhaps ever given a man. Ardent dreams of reformation were scattered to the winds, and he had to face a fruitless labour and the sense that he was increasing the evil he strove against, the exact opposite of the commission to open men’s eyes and turn them from darkness to light. He observes that the words were afterwards quoted by Christ and by two apostles as fulfilled in their own work, and that the prophet had the support of knowing the failure would not be total, since a remnant should be saved; he hears a touch of scorn in the phrase this people.

Matthew Henry says God took the prophet at his word and sent him on a strange errand, to foretell the ruin of his people and even to ripen them for it; he counts the passage quoted or referred to six times in the New Testament, taking this to show that such judgments fall most often in gospel times and that, though they make the least noise, they are the most dreadful. Calvin reads the warning as armour: the prophet needed fortifying like a brazen wall against a stubbornness he would meet for more than sixty years, and God forewarns him so that the event might not terrify him as something strange, bidding him teach without regard to the effect, since the teaching is commanded and the consequences are God’s. Wesley meets the difficulty of the imperative form, which he says is not a command of what the people ought to do but a prediction of what they would do: their sin shall be their punishment, the word continuing while the Spirit is withdrawn, so that they shall be as unable as they are now unwilling to understand. Adam Clarke contributes two manuscript variants and no more.
10:
John Gill offers three readings of the command to make the heart fat: the gospel does it through the wickedness of man’s heart, being a savour of death unto death to some, as the sun hardens clay; or the prophet is to declare their hearts already gross; or God gives them up to a judicial hardness. Adam Clarke presses the first distinction hardest: the prophet speaks of the event, not of God’s purpose and act by his ministry, and prophets are elsewhere said to perform what they only foretell — one is charged over nations to pluck up and pull down, another says he came to destroy the city when he means he came to prophesy its destruction. He also allows a plainer idiom: ye certainly hear, but do not understand; ye certainly see, but do not acknowledge. John Wesley settles it briefly: the hardening is ascribed to the prophet because God inflicted it by his ministry, partly by foretelling what the preaching would produce and partly by withdrawing the light and help of his Spirit; they were made unable to see because they had first been unwilling.

To hear and not understand, Clarke notices, is a common saying in many languages: Demosthenes uses it and expressly calls it a proverb, Aeschylus has seeing they saw in vain and hearing they did not understand, and the prophet raises it into something with the air of poetry. Charles Ellicott ranges wider. The thought is the hardening of Pharaoh’s heart and of Sihon, the headstrong will that defies restraint; the poets of Greece recognised a judicial blindness following on sinful deeds; the mediaeval adage that whom God wishes to destroy he first drives mad states one aspect of the same law, though the wishing to destroy is excluded by clearer revelation of a God not willing that any should perish. To shut the eyes is literally to daub or besmear, perhaps pointing to the practice of closing them as a punishment, a son of the Great Mogul having been so treated by his father; and with Cheyne he reaches for Shakespeare, that when we in our viciousness grow hard the wise gods seal our eyes.

John Calvin takes the darkest part as doctrine of perpetual use. The prophet is told beforehand that his teaching will not merely be fruitless but will blind the people, and yet that these labours, bringing death and ruin, are an acceptable sacrifice. Every faithful minister meets the same result, and Satan excites his followers to raise a dislike of instruction on the pretence that it is injurious, and that the world has only grown worse by the preaching of it.

Keil and Delitzsch say he heard this with sighing and yet with obedience, and that his question how long was forced from him by sympathy with his own nation, warranted by the certainty that a God true to his promises could not cast off his people for ever. Gill asks it of the blindness and impenitence: how long must they remain. Ellicott hears the question ever on the lips of those facing the mystery of evil, sin permitted to work fresh evil as its punishment and yet remaining evil; a later prophet cried it near the close of the exile, and the souls beneath the altar cry it still. The answer meets him within his own horizon: stroke after stroke until the sin has been adequately punished, though the darkness does not exclude a glimmer of eternal hope. Calvin makes the prayer a lesson in the twofold character a prophet must sustain, unshaken in proclaiming judgment yet not devoid of compassion for brethren whose destruction his office obliges him to foretell, as Jeremiah first complained of his task and afterwards revived his courage. Wesley calls it an abrupt speech of great passion and astonishment, and dates the desolation first by the Babylonians and afterward by the Romans.
12:
John Gill insists the removal is not to Babylon but to the ends of the earth by means of the Romans, who were only instruments of the dispersion; it was the Lord’s doing, a judgment for sin. Charles Ellicott looks instead to the deportation policy of the Assyrian kings, and makes the verse programmatic: from the first hour of the call, exile and return were the key-note of this prophet’s teaching, all his later work a development of that germ, the horizon widening until another empire appears as the instrument of punishment. He renders the great forsaking as great shall be the deserted space, connecting it with what he had heard from the lips of Micah. John Calvin finds nothing new, only the former verse again: survivors of the war are led into captivity and the land left bereft, some fleeing, some banished, some perishing by the sword — the reward of obstinate men who add crime to crime until the indignation of God cannot be appeased. John Wesley adds only that houses and lands are forsaken of their owners.

The tenth is the one hopeful word, and the voices divide over it. Gill reports that some make it ten kings reigning from this death to the captivity, a list Kimchi gives from Jotham to Zedekiah; but taking the prophecy to respect the present dispersion rather than Babylon, he reads the tenth as a remnant according to the election of grace, with the Targum agreeing. Calvin lays out both ways, the Hebrew forms differing only slightly. The ten-kings reading promises a truce, and the number does run from Uzziah to Zedekiah; the prophet would gain no small credit by naming how many should reign after his death. Yet Calvin half prefers the other, that the people keep a hidden vigour and can sprout though they appear entirely dead, as trees renew their foliage when winter is past — then expounds by the ten kings anyway.

Adam Clarke thinks the accomplishment has made the passage clear. When Nebuchadnezzar carried away the greater and better part, a tenth was left, the poorer sort kept as vinedressers and husbandmen under Gedaliah, and the dispersed gathered back to him; yet these fled into Egypt after his death, against the warning given by Jeremiah, and perished there. In the second completion the commonwealth was dissolved by the Romans; the nation grew numerous again out of the scanty residue, and Hadrian slew half a million more, almost extirpating it. After all these destructions, Clarke says, we yet see with astonishment that the stock still remains, from which God will make his people shoot forth again.

Ellicott reads it harder before he reads it softer: though there should be a tenth in it, yet this shall be again devoured with fire, successive chastisements sifting the people till only the chosen remnant is left, the tenth being an ideally consecrated portion. The teil tree he corrects to terebinth, and the casting of leaves to being cut down. The tree may be stripped and lopped, nothing left but the stump; and out of that dead-seeming stock, pruned by the chastisements of God, a young shoot springs, holy because consecrated, carrying on the nation’s life — the thought governing the apostle’s hope that first the remnant and then all Israel should be saved, and which applied to the house of David becomes essentially Messianic. Keil and Delitzsch add a technical footnote denying that the word can mean plant; of a tree deprived of its crown it can only mean the stump. Wesley keeps the remnant indefinite and reads two devourings, by the kings of Syria and then by the Romans, before a last holy seed that shall look upon him whom they have pierced and mourn; the leaves are cast in winter, but a vital principle keeps life in the root and in due time sends it into every branch.
